Case Vignette: Mr. A., Age 61

Mr. A. is a 61-year-old South Asian man, a married father of three adult children, who has worked as a paramedic for thirty-four years. He presents for therapy at the urging of his wife, who has grown increasingly worried about his withdrawal and irritability over the past eighteen months.

He tells his story slowly, often pausing to rub his temples. The event that changed everything happened on a humid July afternoon, two years ago. He and his partner were first on scene at a small industrial warehouse fire. The call had come in as a "minor chemical spill," but when they arrived, the air was thick with a sweet, acrid smell that burned his nostrils immediately. The scene was chaotic—workers were coughing, eyes streaming, some vomiting. Mr. A. did what he had always done: he moved into the hot zone without a second thought to pull a dazed man to safety. He remembers the feeling of the slick, oily residue on his gloves, the way it soaked through his uniform at the knees. He was decontaminated on scene, but the smell stayed with him for days.

For the first six months afterward, he noticed nothing unusual. He was proud of the save. Then the nightmares started. They are not replays of the fire, but fragmented, sensory assaults—the taste of metal in his mouth, the sensation of his skin crawling, the sound of his own ragged breathing inside his respirator. He wakes up drenched in sweat, convinced he can smell that sweet chemical odor on his pillow. His wife says he sometimes cries out in his sleep, words she cannot understand.

The most difficult change, he says, is what he calls "the vigilance." On the job, he now finds himself scanning every call for hidden hazards. A simple kitchen grease fire makes his heart pound. He checks his PPE three times before entering a scene, a behavior his younger partner finds excessive. He has started to avoid certain dispatch codes entirely, trading shifts with colleagues to avoid "chemical" or "industrial" calls. Last month, he refused to enter a garage where a car battery had exploded, citing "safety concerns," though he knew it was safe. He felt a hot wave of shame as a rookie paramedic walked past him.

At home, he is a ghost. He used to cook elaborate South Indian meals for his family on weekends; now he eats alone, often standing in the kitchen, because sitting at the table makes him feel trapped. He has stopped attending his grandson's soccer games. The noise of the crowd, the smell of the grass, the sudden shouts—they all feel like an ambush. He tells his wife he is just tired, but the truth is he feels a constant, low-grade dread, as if his body is waiting for the next toxic cloud to appear. He finds himself driving home from work via a longer route that avoids the industrial district, even though it adds twenty minutes to his commute.

His PCL-5 score is 35, reflecting a moderate level of distress. He describes feeling "hollow" rather than sad. He is not suicidal, but he admits, "If the ambulance went off a bridge tomorrow, I wouldn't be too upset." He still goes to work every day, but he describes it as "acting" like a paramedic. He feels disconnected from the man he used to be—the one who ran toward danger without hesitation. He worries his colleagues see him as "broken," and he refuses to speak to his union about his symptoms, fearing he will lose his license. He spends his days off in the garage, organizing his tools, a task he finds numbing. He has not told anyone the full story of that July afternoon, not even his wife. He says he doesn't want to be a burden.
